It's thirty-three degrees outside right now. / In Latvia. / In June. 

That sentence shouldn't make sense, right? 

The average temperature in June here is twenty-one degrees. / I'm sitting in a room that wasn't built for this / because nobody built rooms here for this. 

Latvia wasn’t built for air conditioning. / We didn’t have a plan. / All we suddenly experience is just heat. 

And that's the thing I keep coming back to. / This stopped being a surprise years ago. / So why does it keep catching us completely unprepared? 

Europe just lived through one of the worst heat waves ever recorded. / And I don't mean that loosely. 

France hit its highest nationally averaged temperature since records began in nineteen forty-seven.  

One town in western France / a place called Pissos / recorded forty-four point three degrees Celsius. / Bordeaux hit forty-one. / Nearly half of mainland France was placed under a red heat alert. 

Spain hit forty-five degrees in the south. / The hottest June on record for the country since nineteen fifty. / Germany reached forty degrees / and some of its autobahns buckled under the heat. / Actual roads. / Warping and cracking in the sun. 

The U.K. broke its June temperature record. / The village of Santon Downham in Suffolk hit thirty-seven point three degrees / beating a record that had stood since nineteen seventy-six. 

Switzerland registered its hottest ever June temperature. / Belgium set an electricity price record / of over one euro per kilowatt hour / because every air conditioner that exists on the continent / turned on at the same moment / and the power grid couldn't take it. 

The Eiffel Tower closed early. / Also, the Louvre closed. / Paris Pride was cancelled. / Dozens of schools across England shut for three days. / Rail operator Deutsche Bahn in Germany told people / simply / not to travel. 

A six hundred metre freight train in Sweden derailed / because the tracks warped from the heat. 

This wasn't just uncomfortable. / It was a structural failure. / Across an entire continent. / Simultaneously. 

The W.H.O. confirmed more than thirteen hundred excess deaths / just since June twenty first. / That number will go up as final mortality data comes in / because excess death counts always lag by weeks. 

France alone recorded around one thousand more deaths than expected / between June twenty fourth and June twenty eighth. / Spain's mortality monitoring system linked over three hundred deaths to the heat wave / in the first week alone. 

At least forty-eight people drowned in France / swimming in unsupervised rivers and lakes / trying to cool down. / Forty-eight people. / Dead. / Because they were too hot / and there was nowhere safe to go. 

A twenty-one-year-old professional footballer / Kenzo Kies / drowned in the Rhône River. / His club Guingamp confirmed his death. / He was trying to cool off. 

Two children / a two-year-old and a four-year-old / were found unconscious in a family car / in a town called Carpentras / in southeastern France. / Three elderly people in the Bordeaux region / aged eighty to ninety-five / died from heat related causes / in the same week. 

These aren't statistics from a war zone. / These are from a Tuesday in June / in one of the wealthiest, most developed regions of the planet. 

And the W.H.O. went even further. / They estimated that extreme heat has killed roughly two hundred thousand people across Europe / in the last four years alone. 

Here's the thing. / This isn't new. 

Europe has known it's warming faster than anywhere else for years. / The Copernicus Climate Change Service confirmed it / Europe is warming twice as fast as the global average. / It's the fastest warming continent in the world. / Second only to the Arctic. 

And yet. / Only twenty percent of European homes have air conditioning. / Just some Twenty percent. 

In the United States that number is ninety percent. / In Japan it's ninety one percent. / Canada / which has a colder overall climate than most of Europe / sits at nearly seventy percent. / Europe is at twenty. / And that average hides even worse numbers underneath it. 

In Germany it's about three percent. / In the U.K. / it's around five percent. / And only three percent of U.K. households where someone over seventy-five lives / have any cooling at all. 

The people most likely to die from heat / are the least likely to have protection from it. 

So why hasn't Europe fixed this? / The answer is complicated / and honestly / a little bit maddening. 

The first reason is historical. / Most European buildings were designed to solve the opposite problem. / They were built to retain heat. / Thick stone walls. / Small windows. / Heavy insulation. 

A professor at Cambridge put it simply: / "It's designed to solve a very opposite problem." / Old buildings weren't built with cooling in mind / because for most of European history / you didn't need to cool them. 

In England / one in six homes was built before nineteen hundred. / You cannot easily retrofit central cooling into a nineteenth century terraced house. / The pipes aren't there. / The structural layout wasn't planned for it. 

It's not impossible / but it's expensive / and it takes time / and most people can't afford to do it alone. 

The second reason is a policy trap / and this one's almost darkly funny. / The E.U. is extremely mindful of its climate commitments. / So, while governments quietly know that air conditioning is becoming a public health necessity / they can't officially push for it / because mass air conditioning adoption would massively increase energy demand / which would blow up their carbon targets. 

So, the official answer is / shade trees. / Better building codes for new construction. / And cooling centres. 

The community hall. / If you can get there. / If you're not elderly and alone and confused and the only advice you've received is / drink water and close your curtains. 

Here's where it gets genuinely uncomfortable. / Because the solutions aren't clean. 

If every European home installs air conditioning / energy demand spikes. / Most of that energy still comes partly from fossil fuels. / More fossil fuels equal to more warming. / More warming means more heat waves. 

And more heat waves means more air conditioning. / It's all just a loop. / And there's no easy exit from it. 

Experts at Oxford and Cambridge are proposing passive cooling solutions instead. / Green roofs. / Urban trees. / Reflective building materials. / Better ventilation design in new builds. 

One analysis found that combining these approaches could lower indoor temperatures by up to two point nine degrees. 

Which sounds small / until you remember that the difference between thirty-nine degrees and forty-two degrees / is sometimes the difference between surviving a heat wave / and not. 

Those solutions take decades. / They require new buildings and new planning codes. 

Some political will sustained across multiple election cycles. / None of which Europe has shown it can do when heat comes every summer. And politics reset every four years. 

So, we're stuck in a very specific kind of modern failure. 

Where we know exactly what's happening. And we have the science; we have the data. / We can model the deaths before they occur. / And yet, we still can't move fast enough / to stop them from occurring. 

Which brings me back to my room. Back to right now. / Here in Latvia / the national meteorology centre issued an orange heat alert for this weekend. / They forecast tropical nights / where the temperature doesn't drop below twenty degrees / for the first time in recorded Latvian history. 

The last time Latvia saw a June this hot was all the way back in nineteen seventy-three. June twenty-eighth, to be exact. A thirty-four-point six-degree spike in a little coastal town called Mērsrags. 

That date is today. / Right now / as this video goes out / Latvia is either matching or breaking a fifty-three-year-old record. 

And the Latvian official guidance is to avoid sun exposure between noon and four. / To drink fluids. / Don't leave children or animals in cars. 

That's it. / That's the plan for a country that's never had to think about this before. / Which is fine / because it's the only plan available / when the infrastructure was never built for the question being asked. 

I'm not going to pretend I have a clean answer here. / I don't think anyone does. / Installing air conditioning everywhere burns energy. / Not installing it burns people. / Building passive cooling infrastructure takes thirty years. / The heat is here now. 

What I keep thinking about is that this is the same structure we keep seeing / in every other part of life. / The system was built for a world that no longer exists. / And the people living inside it / just get told to cope. / Drink water. / Close your curtains. / Figure it out. 

The thing is / the curtains don't work anymore. / And I think quietly / everyone already knows that. 

Stay safe out there. / I'll see you in the next one.

Life isn't about waiting for the perfect moment.
It's about creating it.
Sometimes that means taking a step into the unknown.
Trusting your instincts and seeing where the path leads.
Every challenge we face is just an opportunity to grow a little wiser, stronger and more resilient.
So, take a deep breath, embrace the journey and make today count.
